title: Short Stuff: Chinese Food on Christmas
summary: Short Stuff episode on the tradition of eating Chinese food on Christmas. Josh and Chuck (with guest-sitting producer Jerry) open with A Christmas Story's restaurant scene and note the absence of Jewish diners. They discuss Elena Kagan's Supreme Court confirmation hearing quip about Jews and Chinese restaurants on Christmas, and Chuck Schumer's explanation that it was likely the only place open. The hosts cover why Chinese food suits kosher-observant Jews (no dairy, few cream or cheese sauces), the role of Chinese restaurants as one of few kosher-friendly options before the mid-century kosher food market, and similarities between Chinese and Eastern European Jewish dishes such as dumplings and pancakes. They trace the tradition's origins to the Lower East Side of Manhattan around the turn of the 20th century, citing Jennifer 8. Lee and the shared experience of two large non-Christian immigrant groups. They describe how Jewish families moved to outer boroughs and suburbs and Chinese restaurants followed, the restaurant's welcoming atmosphere to all customers, Americanized dishes like egg foo young and chop suey, and the modern popularity of General Tso's chicken and Chinese takeout on Christmas. They close by promising a future short stuff on chop suey's origin.

segments.title: Opening banter: A Christmas Story and the empty Chinese restaurant

segments.title: Why Jews eat Chinese food on Christmas
segments.summary: Elena Kagan's confirmation hearing quip and Chuck Schumer's explanation are discussed. The hosts explain that Chinese food is compatible with kosher practice because it lacks dairy, and that Chinese restaurants were one of few places where Jewish Americans could confidently eat kosher before the mid-century kosher food market grew. They also note similarities between Chinese and Eastern European Jewish dishes.
topics: Elena Kagan confirmation hearing Chinese restaurant quip
Jewish Chinese food similarities dumplings blintzes

segments.title: Origins on the Lower East Side
segments.summary: The hosts trace the tradition to the Lower East Side of New York around the turn of the 20th century, citing Jennifer 8. Lee's point that Jewish and Chinese immigrants, the two largest non-Christian immigrant groups, shared the neighborhood and experience of otherness. They also note that Christmas closures of other restaurants left Chinese restaurants open.

segments.title: Spread to the suburbs and Americanized dishes
segments.summary: The hosts describe how Chinese restaurants were welcoming to all customers, how Jewish families moved to other boroughs and suburbs and Chinese restaurants followed, and how Americanized dishes such as egg foo young and chop suey appeared in Jewish cookbooks. They cite a count of about forty thousand Chinese restaurants in the US.

segments.title: General Tso's chicken, personal stories and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss General Tso's chicken as the most popular Christmas Chinese order, share personal Christmas Chinese food memories, mention a future short stuff on chop suey, and close the episode.
